questions.q: Which statement is true for all complex numbers z₁ and z₂?
o: the conjugate of z₁z₂ equals z̄₁·z̄₂
questions.x: Conjugation respects products: the conjugate of z₁z₂ is z̄₁z̄₂. The others fail: for z₁ = 1, z₂ = i, |1 + i| = √2 ≠ 2 and |1 − i| = √2 ≠ 0; for z₁ = z₂ = i, Re(i·i) = −1 but Re(i)·Re(i) = 0.

questions.q: P(S) denotes the power set of a set S and ∅ is the empty set. How many elements does P(P(∅)) have?
questions.x: P(∅) = {∅} has 1 element, so its power set has 2¹ = 2 elements: ∅ and {∅}. Thinking P(∅) is empty gives P(P(∅)) = {∅}, with only 1 element.

questions.q: What is the domain of f(x) = ln(5 − x) + √(x + 1)?
questions.x: ln needs 5 − x > 0, so x < 5; the root needs x + 1 ≥ 0, so x ≥ −1. Together [−1, 5): x = −1 is allowed (√0 = 0) but x = 5 is not (ln 0 is undefined).

questions.q: What is the period of y = tan 3x?
questions.x: tan has period π, so tan 3x repeats when 3x increases by π, that is when x increases by π/3. 2π/3 would use 2π, the period of sin and cos.

questions.q: At which of these points is f(x) = tan x discontinuous?
questions.x: tan x = sin x/cos x is undefined where cos x = 0, for example at x = π/2, so it is discontinuous there. At 0, π and π/4, cos x ≠ 0 and tan x is continuous.

questions.q: A is a 2 × 3 matrix and B is a 3 × 4 matrix. What is the order of AB?
questions.x: AB is defined because A has 3 columns and B has 3 rows; the product has the rows of A and the columns of B: 2 × 4. It is BA that is not defined (4 columns against 2 rows).

questions.q: A shop's daily profit from selling x items is P = −2x² + 80x − 300 rupees. Which number of items gives the greatest profit, and what is that profit?
questions.x: The maximum is at x = −b/(2a) = −80/(−4) = 20, and P(20) = −800 + 1600 − 300 = 500. Check: P = −2(x − 20)² + 500. Leaving out the −300 gives Rs. 800, and using −b/a gives 40.

questions.q: What are the roots of 6x² − x − 2 = 0?
questions.x: Split the middle term: 6x² − 4x + 3x − 2 = (2x + 1)(3x − 2) = 0, so x = −1/2 or x = 2/3. Check: sum 1/6 = −(−1)/6 and product −1/3 = −2/6. Getting the signs of the factors the wrong way round gives 1/2 and −2/3.

questions.q: Resolve (x³ + 1)/(x(x² + 1)) into partial fractions.
questions.x: The fraction is improper: x³ + 1 = (x³ + x) + (1 − x), so it is 1 + (1 − x)/(x(x² + 1)). Then 1 − x = A(x² + 1) + (Bx + C)x gives A = 1, B = −1, C = −1. Check at x = 1: 2/2 = 1 and 1 + 1 − 2/2 = 1. Leaving out the polynomial part 1 is the usual slip.

questions.q: Which term of the H.P. 1/2, 2/9, 1/7, … is 1/27?
questions.x: The reciprocals 2, 9/2, 7 form an A.P. with d = 5/2. Solve 2 + (n − 1)(5/2) = 27: n − 1 = 10, so n = 11. Check: 2 + 25 = 27. Stopping at n − 1 gives the 10th.

questions.q: With how many zeros does 25! end?
questions.x: Each final zero needs a factor 10 = 2 × 5, and factors 5 are the scarcer. The multiples of 5 up to 25 give 25/5 = 5 fives, and 25 = 5² gives one more, so there are 6 zeros. Forgetting the extra 5 in 25 gives 5.

questions.q: What is the greatest positive integer that divides 3^(2n + 2) − 8n − 9 for every positive integer n?
questions.x: n = 1 gives 81 − 17 = 64 and n = 2 gives 729 − 25 = 704 = 64 × 11, so the answer cannot exceed 64. Induction confirms 64 always divides it: 3^(2k + 4) − 8(k + 1) − 9 = 9[3^(2k + 2) − 8k − 9] + 64k + 64. 32 and 8 also divide it but are not the greatest; 128 does not divide 64.

questions.q: For |x| < 1, the second term in the expansion of (1 + x)^(−1/2) is:
questions.x: (1 + x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + … with n = −1/2, so the second term is −x/2. 3x²/8 is the third term, and x/2 drops the minus sign of the index.

questions.q: α lies in the second quadrant with sin α = 5/13, and β lies in the fourth quadrant with cos β = 3/5. What is tan(α − β)?
For angles where it is defined, (sin 3x + sin x)/sin 2x equals:
questions.x: sin 3x + sin x = 2 sin 2x cos x, so dividing by sin 2x leaves 2 cos x. Check x = 30°: (1 + 1/2)/(√3/2) = √3 = 2 cos 30°.

questions.q: What is the least value of y = 5 + 4 sin 3x?
questions.x: sin 3x ≥ −1, so y ≥ 5 − 4 = 1, reached when sin 3x = −1. The factor 3 inside changes the period, not the least value; 9 is the greatest value.

questions.q: A right-angled triangle has hypotenuse 10 and one acute angle 30°. What is its area?
questions.x: The legs are 10 sin 30° = 5 and 10 cos 30° = 5√3, so the area is ½ × 5 × 5√3 = 25√3/2. Forgetting the ½ gives 25√3.

questions.q: The graph of y = cos⁻¹x can be obtained from the graph of y = sin⁻¹x by:
o: shifting it up by π/2 only
reflecting it in the y-axis only
reflecting it in the x-axis, then shifting it up by π/2
reflecting it in the line y = x
questions.x: cos⁻¹x = π/2 − sin⁻¹x: reflecting in the x-axis gives y = −sin⁻¹x, and shifting up by π/2 gives y = π/2 − sin⁻¹x. A shift alone gives π/2 + sin⁻¹x, and reflecting in y = x gives the sine curve.

questions.q: How many solutions does cos θ = −0.3 have in the interval 0 ≤ θ < 2π?
questions.x: Since −1 < −0.3 < 1, the line y = −0.3 cuts one full wave of y = cos θ twice: once in the second quadrant and once in the third, where cosine is negative.

questions.q: What is the local maximum value of f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 1?
questions.x: f′(x) = 3x² − 12x + 9 = 3(x − 1)(x − 3); f″(x) = 6x − 12 is negative at x = 1, so the local maximum is f(1) = 1 − 6 + 9 + 1 = 5. The local minimum value is f(3) = 1, and 3 is where it occurs.

questions.q: The radius of a sphere is measured with an error of 1%. The approximate percentage error in the calculated volume is:
questions.x: V = (4/3)πr³, so dV = 4πr² dr and dV/V = 3 dr/r = 3 × 1% = 3%. The power of r multiplies the percentage error; 2% would be for the surface area 4πr².

questions.q: ∫ sec x dx equals:
questions.x: Multiply above and below by (sec x + tan x): the numerator sec²x + sec x tan x is the derivative of the denominator, giving ln|sec x + tan x| + C. ln|sec x| + C is ∫ tan x dx, and ln|cosec x − cot x| + C is ∫ cosec x dx.

questions.q: ∫ sin 3x cos x dx equals:
questions.x: 2 sin 3x cos x = sin 4x + sin 2x, so the integral is ½∫(sin 4x + sin 2x) dx = ½(−cos 4x/4 − cos 2x/2) + C = −(cos 4x)/8 − (cos 2x)/4 + C. Leaving out the ½ gives −(cos 4x)/4 − (cos 2x)/2.

questions.q: What is the general solution of dy/dx + y = 1?
questions.x: Separate: dy/(1 − y) = dx, so −ln|1 − y| = x + k and 1 − y = Ae^(−x); hence y = 1 + ce^(−x). Check: y′ = −ce^(−x), so y′ + y = 1.

questions.q: What is the centroid of the triangle with vertices (1, 2), (3, −4) and (5, 8)?
questions.x: Centroid = ((1 + 3 + 5)/3, (2 − 4 + 8)/3) = (3, 2). Forgetting to divide by 3 gives (9, 6).

questions.q: Where do the lines 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2 intersect?
questions.x: Adding the equations gives 3x = 9, so x = 3 and then y = 1. Check: 6 + 1 = 7 and 3 − 1 = 2.

questions.q: A(−3, 0) and B(3, 0) are the ends of a diameter of x² + y² = 9, and P(x, y) is any other point on the circle. What is (slope of PA) × (slope of PB)?
questions.x: The slopes are y/(x + 3) and y/(x − 3), with product y²/(x² − 9). On the circle y² = 9 − x², so the product is −1: the angle in a semicircle is a right angle.

questions.q: For the parabola x² = −6y, which statement is correct?
o: Its axis is y = 0 and it opens to the left
Its axis is x = 0 and it opens downward
Its axis is x = 0 and it opens upward
Its axis is y = 0 and it opens to the right
questions.x: x² = −4ay with 4a = 6: every point has y ≤ 0, so it opens downward and is symmetric about the y-axis (x = 0). Its focus is (0, −3/2).

questions.q: What is the unit vector in the direction of a + b, where a = 2i + 2j − 5k and b = 2i + j + 3k?
questions.x: a + b = 4i + 3j − 2k, whose magnitude is √(16 + 9 + 4) = √29, so the unit vector is (4i + 3j − 2k)/√29. Dividing by 5 ignores the k-part.

questions.q: Use the trapezium rule with h = 1 to estimate ∫₀⁴ √x dx.
questions.x: The ordinates are 0, 1, √2, √3, 2, so the estimate is ½[0 + 2 + 2(1 + √2 + √3)] = 2 + √2 + √3, about 5.15, a little below the exact 16/3. Forgetting the ½ gives 4 + 2√2 + 2√3.

questions.q: A living cell has a volume of 1000 μm³. Its volume in cubic metres is:
questions.x: 1 μm³ = (10⁻⁶ m)³ = 10⁻¹⁸ m³, so 1000 μm³ = 10³ × 10⁻¹⁸ = 10⁻¹⁵ m³. Using 10⁻⁶ without cubing gives 10⁻³ m³; forgetting the 1000 gives 10⁻¹⁸ m³.

questions.q: Vector P = î + 2ĵ and vector Q = 3î + k̂. The vector product P × Q is:
questions.x: P × Q = î(2·1 − 0·0) − ĵ(1·1 − 0·3) + k̂(1·0 − 2·3) = 2î − ĵ − 6k̂. Check: its dot product with P is 2 − 2 + 0 = 0 and with Q is 6 + 0 − 6 = 0. −2î + ĵ + 6k̂ is Q × P, the reversed order.

questions.q: Two forces, each of magnitude F, act at a point with an angle of 120° between them. The magnitude of their resultant is:
questions.x: Take one force along x: components (F, 0) and (F cos 120°, F sin 120°) = (−F/2, √3F/2). Sum = (F/2, √3F/2), magnitude √(F²/4 + 3F²/4) = F. 2F would need the forces to be parallel; √3 F is the result for 60°.

questions.q: A car of mass 1000 kg accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m s⁻¹ in 10 s. The net force on it is:
questions.x: a = (20 − 0)/10 = 2 m s⁻², so F = ma = 1000 × 2 = 2000 N; check: F = Δp/Δt = 20 000/10 = 2000 N. Multiplying mass by the final speed gives 20 000 N (the momentum, not the force).

questions.q: The velocity–time graph of a body moving along a straight line is a straight line from +10 m s⁻¹ at t = 0 to −10 m s⁻¹ at t = 4 s. In these 4 s, the distance travelled and the magnitude of the displacement are:
questions.x: The velocity is zero at t = 2 s. Area from 0 to 2 s = ½ × 10 × 2 = +10 m; from 2 to 4 s = −10 m. Distance = 10 + 10 = 20 m; displacement = 10 − 10 = 0. Adding the areas with their signs for the distance gives zero by mistake.

questions.q: A spring of spring constant 200 N m⁻¹ is already stretched by 0.1 m. The extra work needed to stretch it slowly from an extension of 0.1 m to 0.2 m is:
questions.x: W = ½k(x₂² − x₁²) = ½ × 200 × (0.04 − 0.01) = 3 J (the area of the trapezium under the F–x graph from 20 N to 40 N: ½(20 + 40) × 0.1 = 3 J). Using ½k(Δx)² gives 1 J; stretching from zero to 0.2 m gives 4 J.

questions.q: Two small 1 kg masses are fixed at the ends of a light rod 2 m long. The moment of inertia of the system about an axis through the middle of the rod, perpendicular to it, is:
questions.x: Each mass is 1 m from the axis: I = Σmr² = 1 × 1² + 1 × 1² = 2 kg m². Using the full 2 m length for each mass gives 8 kg m²; 4 kg m² is the value about an axis through one of the masses.

questions.q: A point on a rigid body rotating with angular velocity ω is at a distance r from the axis. Its linear (tangential) speed v is given by:
questions.x: Arc length s = rθ; dividing by time gives v = rω. rω² is the centripetal acceleration, not the speed.

questions.q: Bernoulli's equation for a fluid in steady flow is an application of the law of conservation of:
questions.x: Bernoulli's equation equates the work done by pressure to the changes in kinetic and potential energy per unit volume, so it is conservation of energy. Conservation of mass gives the equation of continuity instead.

questions.q: A microwave oven heats food mainly because:
o: The microwaves heat the metal walls, which then conduct heat to the food
The microwaves become hotter as they are reflected back and forth
The microwaves make water molecules in the food vibrate strongly by resonance, so they absorb energy
The microwaves set up sound waves that rub the food
questions.x: The microwave frequency matches a natural frequency of the water molecules, so they absorb energy strongly (resonance) and the food warms from inside. The metal walls only reflect the microwaves.

questions.q: A car sounding its horn and a cyclist ahead of it move in the same direction along a straight road, both at 10 m s⁻¹, in still air. The frequency heard by the cyclist is:
o: Higher than the frequency of the horn
Lower than the frequency of the horn
Equal to the frequency of the horn
Higher at first and then lower
questions.x: f′ = f(v − u_o)/(v − u_s) with u_o = u_s = 10 m s⁻¹, so f′ = f. There is no relative motion between source and observer, so there is no Doppler shift.

questions.q: A passing gravitational wave changes the length of a 4 km interferometer arm by 1 × 10⁻¹⁸ m. What is the fractional change in length (strain) ΔL/L?
questions.x: ΔL/L = 1 × 10⁻¹⁸/(4 × 10³) = 0.25 × 10⁻²¹ = 2.5 × 10⁻²². Leaving the arm length in kilometres gives 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁹; multiplying instead of dividing gives 4 × 10⁻¹⁵.

questions.q: A wavefront leaves a point source, travels 3 m through air (take it as vacuum) and then 2 m through glass of refractive index 1.5. Taking c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, how long does it take to cover the 5 m?
questions.x: In air t = 3/(3 × 10⁸) = 10 ns; in glass v = c/1.5 = 2 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, so t = 2/(2 × 10⁸) = 10 ns; total 20 ns. Check: optical path = 3 + 1.5 × 2 = 6 m, and 6/c = 20 ns. Ignoring the glass gives 16.7 ns.

questions.q: A child whose near point is 15 cm and an adult whose near point is 30 cm each use a convex lens of focal length 5 cm as a magnifier, with the final image at their own near point. Their magnifying powers are:
o: 7 for the child and 4 for the adult
4 for the child and 7 for the adult
3 for the child and 6 for the adult
questions.x: M = 1 + d/f: child 1 + 15/5 = 4, adult 1 + 30/5 = 7. Someone with a farther near point sees the object smaller without the lens, so the lens helps more. Using d/f alone gives 3 and 6.

questions.q: The molar specific heat of a gas at constant pressure is greater than at constant volume because, at constant pressure:
o: The molecules gain more kinetic energy per kelvin
Heat is lost through the walls
Part of the heat supplied does work as the gas expands
questions.x: At constant volume all the heat raises the internal energy; at constant pressure the gas also expands and does work, so more heat is needed for the same rise in temperature.

questions.q: Three charges of +2 μC each are placed at the corners P, Q and R of an equilateral triangle of side 30 cm. Taking k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², what is the magnitude of the net force on the charge at R?
questions.x: Each force = 9 × 10⁹ × (2 × 10⁻⁶)²/0.09 = 0.4 N, and the two forces at R are 60° apart. Resultant = 2 × 0.4 × cos 30° = 0.4√3 ≈ 0.69 N. Adding them as if in line gives 0.8 N; treating them as at right angles gives 0.4√2 N.

questions.q: In a photocopier, the toner powder sticks to the drum only:
o: Where light from the white parts of the original has fallen
Where the drum is still charged, matching the dark parts of the original
questions.x: The photoconducting drum is charged all over; light reflected from the white parts of the page makes those areas conduct and lose their charge. The charged toner is attracted only to the parts still charged, which match the dark print.

questions.q: The equipotential surfaces around an isolated point charge are:
o: Concentric spheres centred on the charge
Straight lines radiating from the charge
questions.x: V = kq/r is the same at every point the same distance r from the charge, so equipotentials are spheres centred on it. Radial lines are the field lines, which cross the equipotentials at right angles.

questions.q: A 60 W bulb and a 100 W bulb, both rated for 220 V, are connected in series across a 220 V supply. Which statement is correct?
o: The 100 W bulb glows brighter, because it has the higher power rating
The 60 W bulb glows brighter, because it has the larger resistance and the same current flows in both
Both glow equally, because the same current flows in both
The 100 W bulb glows brighter, because it has the larger resistance
questions.x: R = V²/P, so the 60 W bulb has the larger resistance. In series the current is the same, and P = I²R is larger for the larger resistance, so the 60 W bulb is brighter. The rating applies only at the full 220 V across each bulb.

questions.q: A galvanometer of resistance 49 Ω is fitted with a shunt of 1 Ω. When a current of 5 A passes through the combination, the current through the galvanometer is:
questions.x: The galvanometer and shunt share the same p.d., so the current divides inversely with resistance: Ig = 5 × 1/(49 + 1) = 0.1 A. The other 4.9 A passes through the shunt.

questions.q: Ions pass undeflected through a velocity selector with E = 1 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ and B = 0.1 T. They then enter a region where only a uniform magnetic field of 0.1 T acts, at right angles to their velocity, and move in a circle of radius 1 cm. Their charge-to-mass ratio is:
questions.x: From the selector, v = E/B = 10⁴/0.1 = 10⁵ m s⁻¹. In the field r = mv/(qB), so q/m = v/(rB) = 10⁵/(0.01 × 0.1) = 10⁸ C kg⁻¹. Leaving r in centimetres gives 10⁶ C kg⁻¹.

questions.q: A DC motor with armature resistance 1 Ω is connected to a 220 V supply and draws 20 A at its working speed. The mechanical power developed in the armature is:
questions.x: Back emf ε = V − IR = 220 − 20 = 200 V, and mechanical power = εI = 200 × 20 = 4000 W. Check: input VI = 4400 W minus heat I²R = 400 W gives 4000 W. 4.4 kW is the input power.

questions.q: A steady DC supply of 10 V and a sinusoidal AC supply produce heat at the same rate in a given resistor. The peak value of the AC voltage is:
questions.x: Equal heating means the rms value of the AC is 10 V, and V₀ = √2 × V(rms) = 10√2 V (about 14 V). Dividing by √2 instead of multiplying gives 5√2 V.

questions.q: A ferromagnetic specimen is taken repeatedly round its hysteresis loop. The area enclosed by the loop represents:
o: The energy lost as heat per unit volume in each cycle
The magnetic flux density left when the field is removed
The field needed to demagnetise the specimen
questions.x: The area of the B–H loop equals the energy dissipated as heat per unit volume per cycle of magnetisation. The flux density left at zero field is the retentivity, and the reverse field needed to remove it is the coercivity; these are points on the loop, not its area.

questions.q: A half-wave rectifier uses one silicon diode (forward drop 0.7 V). The AC input to the diode has a peak value of 10 V. The peak voltage across the load resistor is about:
questions.x: At the peak the diode conducts and drops 0.7 V, so the load gets 10 − 0.7 = 9.3 V. Ignoring the drop gives 10 V; adding it gives 10.7 V; 7.1 V is the rms value of a 10 V peak, not the peak output.

questions.q: Muons made high in the atmosphere reach the ground in large numbers although their lifetime is very short. In the muons' own frame of reference, they reach the ground because:
o: The thickness of the atmosphere is contracted
questions.x: In the muons' rest frame their lifetime is the normal short one, but the atmosphere rushes past at nearly c, so its thickness is length-contracted and is covered in that short time. Time dilation of the lifetime is the explanation from the Earth's frame, not from the muons' frame.

questions.q: A perfect black body is a body that:
o: Reflects all the radiation that falls on it
Emits radiation of one wavelength only
Absorbs all the radiation that falls on it, whatever its wavelength
questions.x: A black body absorbs every wavelength completely, reflecting none; it is also the best possible emitter at any temperature (a small hole in a hollow enclosure is a good model). It emits a continuous spectrum, not a single wavelength.

questions.q: A hydrogen atom in its ground state (−13.6 eV) absorbs a photon of energy 12.75 eV. Using Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV, the electron is raised to the level:
questions.x: The new energy is −13.6 + 12.75 = −0.85 eV, and −13.6/n² = −0.85 gives n² = 16, n = 4. Check: E₃ = −1.51 eV would need 12.09 eV, and E₅ = −0.54 eV would need 13.06 eV.

questions.q: The dose rate from a small gamma-ray source is 8 μGy per hour at a distance of 1 m. Ignoring absorption in air, the dose rate at 2 m from the source is:
questions.x: Radiation from a point source spreads over a sphere, so intensity ∝ 1/r²: doubling the distance divides the dose rate by 4, giving 8/4 = 2 μGy per hour. Treating it as ∝ 1/r gives 4 μGy per hour. This is why keeping a distance is a key safety rule.

questions.q: In the standard model, two of the four fundamental forces are combined into a single electroweak force. These two forces are:
o: The strong force and the weak force
The electromagnetic force and the weak force
questions.x: At very high energies the electromagnetic force (carried by photons) and the weak force (carried by W⁺, W⁻ and Z⁰) behave as one electroweak force; the Higgs field explains why W and Z are massive while the photon is not. Gravity is not yet unified with the others.

questions.q: In a blast furnace, iron(III) oxide is reduced: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. What mass of iron is obtained from 16 g of Fe₂O₃? (O = 16, Fe = 56)
questions.x: Fe₂O₃ = 160 g mol⁻¹, so 16 g = 0.1 mol, giving 0.2 mol Fe = 0.2 × 56 = 11.2 g. Forgetting the 2 Fe per Fe₂O₃ gives 5.6 g.

questions.q: 0.53 g of anhydrous sodium carbonate is dissolved in water and titrated with 0.10 mol dm⁻³ HCl using methyl orange: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. The volume of acid needed is: (C = 12, O = 16, Na = 23)
questions.x: Na₂CO₃ = 106 g mol⁻¹, so 0.53 g = 0.005 mol; HCl needed = 2 × 0.005 = 0.010 mol; volume = 0.010/0.10 = 0.100 dm³ = 100 cm³. Forgetting the 1 : 2 ratio gives 50 cm³.

questions.q: A fixed amount of an ideal gas has both its pressure and its volume doubled. The average kinetic energy of its molecules:
questions.x: PV = nRT, so doubling both P and V makes PV, and hence T, four times larger. Average kinetic energy ∝ T, so it becomes four times as large. Thinking the two changes cancel gives 'stays the same'.

questions.q: Glycerol, CH₂(OH)CH(OH)CH₂OH, is much more viscous than water. The main reason is that:
o: Each glycerol molecule has three O–H groups and forms many hydrogen bonds with its neighbours
Glycerol molecules move faster than water molecules
questions.x: Three O–H groups per molecule give an extensive hydrogen-bonded network, and the larger molecules also have stronger London forces, so layers resist flowing past each other.

questions.q: Which ion has the same number of electrons as a neon atom (Z = 10) but more protons than electrons? (Z: N 7, O 8, F 9, Na 11)
questions.x: All four ions have 10 electrons. Na⁺ has 11 protons (more than its electrons), while F⁻, O²⁻ and N³⁻ have 9, 8 and 7 protons, fewer than 10 electrons. Mixing up positive and negative ions gives the wrong choices.

questions.q: An atom X has the ground-state configuration [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴. The numbers of unpaired electrons in X and in the ion X²⁻ are:
questions.x: 3p⁴: four electrons in three p orbitals, so one pair and two singles, giving 2 unpaired (Hund's rule). X²⁻ is 3p⁶, all paired, giving 0. Counting all four p electrons as unpaired gives 4.

questions.q: Which molecule is trigonal pyramidal in shape?
questions.x: Phosphorus in PCl₃ has three bond pairs and one lone pair; the four pairs are arranged tetrahedrally and the three Cl atoms form a pyramid. BCl₃, SO₃ and NO₃⁻ have three electron regions and no lone pair on the central atom, so they are trigonal planar; BCl₃ is tempting because its formula looks like PCl₃.

questions.q: The enthalpy of neutralisation of ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, by sodium hydroxide solution is found to be:
o: More negative than −57 kJ mol⁻¹, because the weak acid releases extra energy as it ionises
Less negative than −57 kJ mol⁻¹, because some energy is used to ionise the weak acid
Exactly −57 kJ mol⁻¹, as for every acid and base
Positive, because a weak acid neutralisation absorbs heat
questions.x: −57 kJ mol⁻¹ is for H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l) when the acid is already fully ionised. Ethanoic acid is only slightly ionised, and its ionisation absorbs some of the heat released, so the measured value is a little less negative (about −56 kJ mol⁻¹). Thinking the value is the same for all acids ignores the ionisation step.

questions.q: Iron(III) ions and thiocyanate ions form a blood-red complex: Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ [FeSCN]²⁺(aq). A little FeCl₃ solution is added to the pale red equilibrium mixture. What is seen?
o: The red colour deepens, because the equilibrium shifts to the right
The red colour fades, because the equilibrium shifts to the left
The colour does not change, because Kc is constant
The solution turns colourless, because SCN⁻ is used up completely
questions.x: Adding Fe³⁺ raises a reactant concentration, so the system shifts to the right to use some of it up, forming more red [FeSCN]²⁺. Kc does stay constant, but the position of equilibrium changes, so the colour does change.

questions.q: A sealed glass tube contains a mixture of colourless N₂O₄ and brown NO₂ at constant temperature. Which observation shows that the mixture has reached equilibrium?
o: The colour of the mixture stops changing
questions.x: When equilibrium is reached the concentrations of N₂O₄ and NO₂ stay constant, so measurable properties such as colour and pressure become constant. Both gases are still present, so the mixture is neither colourless nor fully dark.

questions.q: A weak monobasic acid HA has Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵. What is the pH of a 0.10 mol dm⁻³ solution of HA? (ionisation is small)
questions.x: [H⁺] = √(Ka × c) = √(1.0 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.10) = √(1.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, so pH = 3.0. Forgetting the square root gives pH 6.0; treating HA as a strong acid gives pH 1.0.

questions.q: 2.44 g of hydrated barium chloride, BaCl₂·xH₂O, is heated to constant mass, leaving 2.08 g of anhydrous BaCl₂. What is x? (BaCl₂ = 208 g mol⁻¹, H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹)
questions.x: Water lost = 2.44 − 2.08 = 0.36 g = 0.020 mol; BaCl₂ = 2.08/208 = 0.010 mol. Ratio 0.020 : 0.010 = 2, so x = 2. Halving the moles of water by mistake (for example dividing 0.36 by 36) gives the tempting 1.

questions.q: A metal X has molar mass 52 g mol⁻¹. When 0.30 F of electricity is passed through a molten compound of X, 5.2 g of X is deposited at the cathode. What is the charge on the X ion in the compound?
questions.x: Moles of X = 5.2/52 = 0.10 mol, deposited by 0.30 mol of electrons. So each ion takes 3 electrons and the ion is X³⁺. Dividing the wrong way (0.10/0.30) or forgetting the molar mass gives the other values.

questions.q: An alkene is hydrogenated over finely divided nickel. According to the adsorption theory of heterogeneous catalysis, the first step is that:
o: Nickel reacts permanently with hydrogen to form a stable compound
Nickel raises the temperature of the mixture
The reactant molecules are adsorbed on the nickel surface, which weakens their bonds
Nickel dissolves in the alkene to form a single phase
questions.x: Reactants are adsorbed on active sites of the metal surface, their bonds weaken and they react; the product then desorbs and the nickel is left unchanged. Finely divided metal works better because it has more surface.

questions.q: In the vapour just above its sublimation temperature, aluminium chloride exists mainly as:
o: Long polymeric chains of AlCl₃ units
A giant covalent network like that of SiO₂
questions.x: Aluminium chloride is covalent; in the vapour two AlCl₃ units join through two Cl bridges (coordinate bonds) to give Al₂Cl₆. This dimer breaks into AlCl₃ only at much higher temperatures. Ions would mean an ionic compound like NaCl or MgCl₂.

questions.q: Which Group 2 metal does not react with water or steam, even at red heat?
questions.x: Beryllium is the least reactive Group 2 metal and does not react with water even as steam. Magnesium reacts with steam (and slowly with hot water), while calcium and barium react with cold water; reactivity rises down the group.

questions.q: Solid orthoboric acid, H₃BO₃, is soft, slippery and flaky. This is because in the crystal:
o: B³⁺ and OH⁻ ions form a strong ionic lattice
Boron and oxygen atoms form a three-dimensional giant covalent network
Boron atoms are held together by metallic bonding
Planar B(OH)₃ units are joined by hydrogen bonds into layers, and the layers are held together only weakly
questions.x: In boric acid each planar B(OH)₃ unit is hydrogen-bonded to its neighbours within a sheet, and the sheets are held by weak forces, so they slide over each other like graphite. An ionic or giant covalent lattice would give a hard, high-melting solid, the most tempting slip.

questions.q: In the laboratory, phosphorus pentoxide (P₄O₁₀) is used mainly as:
o: A powerful drying and dehydrating agent
questions.x: P₄O₁₀ combines very strongly with water to form phosphoric acids, so it is used to dry gases and to dehydrate compounds. Phosphorus is already in its highest (+5) state in it, so it cannot act as a reducing agent.

questions.q: The boiling points of the hydrogen halides increase in the order:
questions.x: From HCl to HI, dispersion forces grow with the number of electrons, so the boiling point rises; HF is the exception because strong hydrogen bonding gives it the highest boiling point (about 20 °C). Forgetting the hydrogen bonding in HF gives the simple increasing order.

questions.q: Stainless steel resists rusting because, besides iron and a little carbon, it contains about:
questions.x: Chromium forms a thin, self-repairing Cr₂O₃ film on the surface, and nickel adds toughness; the common grade is 18/8 Cr/Ni steel. Copper and zinc are the metals of brass, the tempting slip.

questions.q: The IUPAC name of CH₂=CHCH₂OH is:
questions.x: The OH group is the principal group (suffix -ol) and gets the lowest number, so C-1 is the CH₂OH carbon and the double bond is between C-2 and C-3: prop-2-en-1-ol. Giving the double bond the lower number gives prop-1-en-3-ol, the most tempting wrong name.

questions.q: When methane is chlorinated in sunlight, a small amount of ethane is found among the products. The ethane forms when:
o: Two methane molecules each lose a hydrogen atom and join
A methyl free radical attacks a methane molecule
A chlorine free radical attacks a methane molecule
Two methyl free radicals join in a chain-termination step
questions.x: CH₃• + CH₃• → C₂H₆ is a termination step that removes two radicals. Cl• + CH₄ only gives CH₃• and HCl, and CH₃• + CH₄ just swaps a hydrogen; picking these confuses propagation with termination.

questions.q: How many structural isomers are there of trichlorobenzene, C₆H₃Cl₃?
questions.x: The possible positions are 1,2,3-, 1,2,4- and 1,3,5-. Other numberings such as 1,2,5- or 1,3,4- are the same compounds as 1,2,4- numbered differently; counting them separately gives too many.

questions.q: Phenylmagnesium bromide, C₆H₅MgBr, reacts with propanone, CH₃COCH₃, and the product is hydrolysed with dilute acid. The product is:
questions.x: The phenyl group adds to the carbonyl carbon of propanone, which already carries two CH₃ groups; hydrolysis gives the tertiary alcohol C₆H₅C(CH₃)₂OH. 1-Phenylpropan-1-ol would come from propanal, an aldehyde.

questions.q: In the Williamson synthesis, C₂H₅O⁻Na⁺ + CH₃Br → C₂H₅OCH₃ + NaBr, the ethoxide ion acts as:
o: An electrophile that adds to the C–Br bond
A base that removes a hydrogen to form an alkene
A nucleophile that replaces bromide by SN2 substitution
A reducing agent that removes bromine
questions.x: The negatively charged oxygen attacks the δ+ carbon of CH₃Br from the back and pushes out Br⁻ in one step. With bromomethane there is no β-hydrogen, so elimination cannot compete.

questions.q: 6.0 g of methanal is heated with concentrated NaOH and reacts completely by the Cannizzaro reaction: 2HCHO + NaOH → CH₃OH + HCOONa. What mass of methanol forms? (HCHO = 30, CH₃OH = 32 g mol⁻¹)
questions.x: 6.0/30 = 0.20 mol HCHO gives 0.10 mol CH₃OH (2:1) = 3.2 g. Ignoring the 2:1 ratio gives 6.4 g; 1.6 g halves twice.

questions.q: Ethanoic acid reacts with phosphorus pentachloride, PCl₅. Besides ethanoyl chloride, the other products are:
questions.x: CH₃COOH + PCl₅ → CH₃COCl + POCl₃ + HCl: the OH is replaced by Cl, the O goes to phosphorus and the H to HCl. Writing water as a by-product is the usual slip; water would hydrolyse the acyl chloride and is not formed.

questions.q: Propanamide, CH₃CH₂CONH₂, is warmed with bromine and aqueous sodium hydroxide (Hofmann degradation). The organic product is:
questions.x: In the Hofmann reaction RCONH₂ + Br₂ + 4NaOH → RNH₂ + Na₂CO₃ + 2NaBr + 2H₂O, the carbonyl carbon is lost as carbonate, so the amine has one carbon fewer: ethylamine. Keeping all three carbons (propylamine) is the usual slip.

questions.q: Glycogen is best described as:
o: The storage polysaccharide of animals, kept in the liver and muscles
The storage polysaccharide of plants, kept in seeds and tubers
The structural polysaccharide of plant cell walls
questions.x: Animals store glucose as glycogen, a highly branched polymer of glucose. Starch is the plant store and cellulose the plant structural material; lactose is the milk sugar.

questions.q: In an oil refinery, cracking is used mainly to:
o: Join small molecules into larger ones for lubricating oil
Break large alkane molecules from heavy fractions into smaller, more useful alkanes and alkenes
Separate crude oil into fractions by boiling point
questions.x: Heavy fractions are in excess, so cracking breaks them into petrol-sized alkanes and alkenes such as ethene for petrochemicals. Separating by boiling point is fractional distillation, the usual mix-up.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the role of the operating system?
o: It is an application program used mainly for typing letters and reports
It is a hardware chip that stores the user's documents permanently
It translates programs written in a high-level language into machine code
It manages the hardware and provides a platform on which application programs run
questions.x: The operating system is system software that controls memory, devices and files, and application programs run on top of it. Translating high-level programs is the job of a compiler or interpreter, not the operating system itself.

questions.q: Which digit can NOT appear in an octal number?
questions.x: Octal is base 8, so it uses only the digits 0 to 7; the digit 8 is not allowed. 7 is the largest valid octal digit.

questions.q: Which statement about the address bus and the data bus is correct?
o: The data bus width sets how many locations can be reached; the address bus width sets how many bits move at once
The address bus width sets how many locations can be reached; the data bus width sets how many bits move at once
Both widths only decide the clock speed of the processor
The address bus carries the data and the data bus carries the addresses
questions.x: More address lines give more distinct addresses (2ⁿ locations), while more data lines carry more bits in each transfer. The swapped statement mixes up the two buses' jobs.

questions.q: In a bus network, why does performance usually drop as more computers are added?
o: All computers share one cable, so there are more collisions and waiting
Each new computer needs its own cable to a central switch
Data has to pass through every computer in a loop
The terminators stop working when more computers join
questions.x: Every computer on a bus uses the same backbone cable, so with more computers more transmissions clash and have to be resent. Passing data through every computer in a loop describes a ring, not a bus.

questions.q: A client-server network grows from 10 clients to 200 clients that all send their requests to the same single server. What problem is most likely?
o: The server becomes a bottleneck and responses slow down
The clients can no longer send requests at all
Each client must now act as a server
The network changes into a ring topology
questions.x: Every request goes to the one server, so as the number of clients grows it has more work than it can handle quickly. The clients can still send requests; they simply wait longer for replies.

questions.q: What is the main reason for joining the computers of an office into a network?
o: To share resources such as files, printers and an Internet connection
To make each computer's processor run faster
To increase the RAM in every computer
To stop computers from needing an operating system
questions.x: Networking lets users share data, printers and an Internet connection and communicate with each other. It does not change a single computer's processor speed or RAM.

questions.q: Which of these is personal data that an organisation must protect?
o: The number of computers in a lab
The average mark of a whole class
The opening time of a library
questions.x: A CNIC number identifies one particular person, so it is personal data protected by privacy rules. A class average or a lab's computer count does not identify anyone.

questions.q: Software owned by a company that keeps its source code secret and sells licences that let people use it is called:
questions.x: Proprietary (closed-source) software is owned by its maker, whose code stays secret, and users pay for a licence. Freeware is also closed but free, while open-source and public domain software are not kept secret.

questions.q: A spam filter is tested on 100 e-mails: 40 are spam and 60 are not. It correctly marks 30 of the spam e-mails and 54 of the others. What is its accuracy?
questions.x: Correct answers are 30 + 54 = 84 out of 100, so accuracy is 84%. 75% (30 of 40) and 90% (54 of 60) each count only one kind of e-mail.

questions.q: The very first block of a blockchain is called the:
questions.x: The genesis block starts the chain and has no previous block to point to. Every later block stores the hash of the block before it.

questions.q: The faint word CONFIDENTIAL must appear behind the text on every page of a document. Which feature is used?
questions.x: A watermark is faint text or a picture placed behind the main text on every page. A page border only draws lines around the edge of the page.

questions.q: The part of a chart that explains which colour or pattern stands for which data series is the:
questions.x: The legend is the key that matches each colour to its series. The axes carry the scales and category labels.

questions.q: A sequential file holds 600 records. Records are read one by one from the start until the wanted one is found. On average, about how many records are read to find a record that is in the file?
questions.x: The wanted record is equally likely to be anywhere in the file, so on average about half the file, 600 ÷ 2 = 300 records, is read. Reaching a record in one read needs direct access, not sequential reading.

questions.q: In the three-level architecture of a DBMS, which level describes how the data is actually stored on disk?
questions.x: The internal level describes storage details such as files and indexes. The conceptual level describes the whole database's tables and relationships, and the external level the views seen by users.

questions.q:
Table Book(BookID, Title, Subject, Price) holds these rows: (1, Algebra, Maths, 450), (2, Optics, Physics, 600), (3, Calculus, Maths, 700), (4, Atoms, Chemistry, 350), (5, Mechanics, Physics, 500), (6, Geometry, Maths, 400).
In an empty column of the query's Field row, `NewPrice: [Price]+50` is typed. When the query runs, what is shown for Optics, and what happens to the Book table?
o: 650 is shown; the table's Price becomes 650
600 is shown; a NewPrice column is added to the table
650 is shown; the table's Price stays 600
An error is shown because NewPrice is not a field
questions.x: A calculated field in a select query is worked out each time the query runs (600 + 50 = 650) and is not stored. Only an update query would change the Price in the table.

questions.q: In an Access query, the criteria under City is `[Enter city name]`. What happens when the query is run?
o: Access asks the user to type a city and shows the records for it
Access shows the records whose City is the text Enter city name
Access shows an error because of the square brackets
Access deletes the records that have an empty City
questions.x: Text in square brackets that is not a field name makes a parameter query: Access shows the text as a prompt and uses the typed value as the criteria. It would be literal text only if typed in quotes.

questions.q: Which data type is used to store a single character such as 'k'?
questions.x: char holds one character (stored as its character code). float and double are for numbers with fractional parts.

questions.q: A C program has a syntax error in one line. What happens when it is compiled?
o: The compiler reports the error and no object file is made until it is fixed
The compiler skips that line and makes the object file
The linker corrects the error automatically
The program runs and stops only when it reaches that line
questions.x: The compiler cannot translate code that breaks the rules of C, so it lists the error and does not produce object code. The linker only joins object code; it never fixes source errors.

questions.q: Which condition is equivalent to `!(p > 0 || q > 0)`?
questions.x: By De Morgan's law, NOT (X OR Y) = (NOT X) AND (NOT Y), and NOT (p > 0) is p <= 0. Changing || to && is needed, so p <= 0 || q <= 0 is wrong; p < 0 forgets the value 0.

questions.q: The built-in functions `sqrt()` and `pow()` are declared in which header file?
questions.x: The mathematical library functions such as sqrt, pow and fabs are declared in math.h. stdio.h declares input/output functions such as printf and scanf.
p > q (10 > 25) is false, so the else block runs: q = 25 - 10 = 15, then p = 10 + 15 = 25. The new value of q is used in the second statement, so 25 25 is wrong.

questions.q: When a `break` statement runs inside a loop, where does control go next?
o: To the next iteration of the same loop
Back to the first line of `main()`
To the loop condition, which is tested again
To the first statement after the loop
questions.x: break ends the loop at once and the program carries on with the statement after it. Going on to the next iteration is what continue does.

questions.q:
What happens when this Python code runs?
```
marks = 72
print(mark + 5)
```
o: It is a syntax error, because a bracket is missing
It stops with a runtime error (NameError), because `mark` has not been defined
questions.x: The variable created is marks, but line 2 uses mark, a name Python has never seen, so the program stops with a NameError when that line runs. The brackets are complete, so it is not a syntax error.

questions.q: In a Tkinter program with `root = tk.Tk()`, which statement shows Marks Calculator in the window's title bar?
questions.x: The window method `title()` sets the title-bar text. A Label widget shows text inside the window, and there is no `label()` method or `Title` widget for this.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
class Bank:
    def __init__(self, bal):
        self.bal = bal
    def deposit(self, amt):
        self.bal += amt
acc = Bank(100)
acc.deposit(50)
acc.deposit(25)
print(acc.bal)
```
questions.x: The object starts with bal = 100, and each `deposit` adds to the same object's attribute: 100 + 50 + 25 = 175. 125 would forget the first deposit.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
a = b = 5
b = b + 1
print(a, b)
```
questions.x: Both names first refer to 5. `b = b + 1` makes `b` refer to a new value, 6, while `a` still refers to 5, so 5 6 is printed. Changing `b` does not change `a`.

questions.q: Insertion sort (descending) takes each element from the left and inserts it into its place in the sorted part before it, largest first. Starting with `[3, 7, 5, 9]`, what is the list just after 5 has been inserted?
questions.x: Inserting 7 before 3 gives [7, 3, 5, 9]; then 5 goes between 7 and 3: [7, 5, 3, 9]. 9 has not been inserted yet, so the fully sorted [9, 7, 5, 3] comes one step later.
lo = 0, hi = 5, mid = 2: 7 < 13, so lo = 3. mid = (3 + 5) // 2 = 4: L[4] is 13, so it returns 4. The function returns the index, not the value 13; 5 would be counting positions from 1.

questions.q: Merge sort keeps splitting a list of 8 elements into halves until every part has a single element. How many levels of splitting are there (8 → 4 + 4 is the first level)?
questions.x: 8 → 4 + 4 (level 1) → four parts of 2 (level 2) → eight parts of 1 (level 3); log₂ 8 = 3. 7 is the number of separate split operations, not levels.

questions.q: A model predicts house prices (in lakh rupees). For three houses the actual prices are 40, 50 and 60 and the predicted prices are 43, 48 and 61. What is the mean absolute error (the average size of the errors, ignoring their signs)?
questions.x: Errors ignoring sign: |43 − 40| = 3, |48 − 50| = 2, |61 − 60| = 1; their mean is 6 / 3 = 2. 0.67 keeps the signs (3 − 2 + 1 = 2, then 2 / 3), which lets errors cancel; 6 is the total, not the mean.

questions.q: The passage mainly explains:
o: why small birds leave cold countries every autumn
how bright city lights have changed the routes birds take
how birds combine several different guides to find their way on long journeys
why pilots should always carry more than one instrument
questions.x: The second paragraph says birds "do not rely on a single guide but carry several", and the rest shows why that makes them "so dependable". The pilot is only a comparison, not the subject.

questions.q: According to the second paragraph, what seems to tell birds which way is north when clouds hide the sun and the stars?
o: The movement of the sun across the sky
The pattern of stars around the pole
The lights of towns below them
A sense of the earth's magnetism
questions.x: The passage says "When clouds hide both, a sense of the earth's magnetism seems to tell them which way is north." The sun and the stars are the very guides the clouds have hidden.

questions.q: Suppose a bird somehow lost its magnetic sense but flew under clear skies. The passage suggests it would most likely:
o: be unable to tell which way is north
have to find its way by smell alone
be drawn off course by city lights
still find its way by using the sun and the stars
questions.x: Because birds carry several guides, one lost guide matters little: the bird "simply leans more heavily on whichever cues remain", and the sun and stars are available on clear days and nights. Being unable to find north contradicts this point about redundancy.

questions.q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "redundancy" most nearly means:
o: having spare guides that can do the same job
the loss of a job because a worker is no longer needed
a long period of rest before a journey
the habit of returning to the same place
questions.x: The pilot "with four" instruments "can afford to lose one", so redundancy here means having spare means that can do the same job. Losing one's job is the word's commoner meaning, not the one used here.

questions.q: The third paragraph mainly serves to:
o: describe how pilots are trained to fly through storms
explain, through a comparison, why having several guides makes the system reliable
introduce a new guide that birds use near home
show that birds usually get lost in bad weather
questions.x: It opens "This redundancy is what makes the system so dependable" and compares birds with a pilot who "can afford to lose one" instrument. It does not say birds usually get lost; the last paragraph says most journeys end "where it should".

questions.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Roundabouts are safer than traffic lights and should replace them everywhere
Traffic lights waste fuel and should be switched off at night
Lights and roundabouts each have strengths and weaknesses, so the choice depends on the crossing
Pedestrians cannot cross safely at any kind of roundabout
questions.x: The passage weighs both tools and ends "Neither tool, then, is simply better. The right choice depends on how much traffic arrives". Roundabouts are not said to be better everywhere: "roundabouts have limits too".

questions.q: According to the passage, why are violent crashes rare at roundabouts?
o: Pedestrians are kept away from the circle
Drivers wait for a light before they enter
Traffic from each road enters in strict turn
Every vehicle has to slow down and turn
questions.x: The third paragraph says "Because every vehicle must slow down and turn, the violent head-on and side impacts ... become rare". Waiting for a light and taking turns describe traffic lights, not roundabouts.

questions.q: It can be inferred that traffic lights would be the better choice for a crossing:
o: on a quiet road where cars arrive only now and then
where engineers want drivers to judge gaps for themselves
beside a school where many children cross on foot
where the main aim is to save fuel late at night
questions.x: Signals "suit crossings where pedestrians need a protected moment to cross", while "a large roundabout can be hard for people on foot". A quiet road is where lights are weakest: drivers sit "facing an empty junction".

questions.q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "glancing" most nearly means:
o: striking at an angle rather than head-on
questions.x: "Glancing" collisions are set against "violent head-on and side impacts", so they strike at an angle and slide off. "Looking quickly" is the common meaning of glance, not the one used for a collision.

questions.q: How does the third paragraph relate to the second?
o: It gives an example that supports the claim made in the second paragraph
It corrects a mistake in the second paragraph's account of signals
It explains why the tool described in the second paragraph was invented
It treats the other tool in the same way, giving its benefits and then its limits
questions.x: The second paragraph gives the strengths of lights and then "Their weakness"; the third, opening "by contrast", gives the strengths of roundabouts and then "roundabouts have limits too". It does not correct the second paragraph, which it leaves standing.
